newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's Kim in fresh gamble over labour law.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's Kim in fresh gamble over labour law.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam, who has the instincts of a political gambler, is set to raise the stakes in a tussle for public opinion over a controversial labour law, analysts said on Thursday.
Political commentators said Kim was also likely to seek a scapegoat for the ruling camp's blunder in causing a public outcry by ramrodding the law through parliament.

"President Kim gambles in a big way, particularly when he is cornered. If he loses over one thing, he will be in another gamble with higher bets," political science professor Cho Chang-hyun of Hanyang University told Reuters.

Analysts who have followed Kim's political career said they were not surprised by his dramatic about-face this week to reopen parliamentary debate over the law that sparked more than three weeks of wildcat strikes.
"The concession is a tactical retreat. Kim hates to lose political control and he will soon launch a new offensive against the opposition," Cho said.
Kim had previously ruled out compromise over the law, saying labour reform was vital to pump life into a sagging economy.

Officials from Kim's ruling New Korea Party said privately that he conceded the law had caused public anxiety and had hurt the economy because public criticism and worker protests were worse than the party had anticipated.
But the opposition rejected Kim's offer for dialogue, saying any parliamentry debate would require dumping the law first.
"It is typical of his strategy to bring about a new phase by making a U-turn," one Asian diplomat said. "He will probably blame everthing on party chairman Lee Hong-koo for the gaffe."
Lee, tipped as a leading presidential candidate, summoned party members to a dawn session of parliament on December 26 to ram the bill through while opposition deputies slept.
Opinion polls have shown Kim's party would lose presidential polls scheduled for December if the labour strife went on.
Kim's biggest gamble was in 1990 when he shocked the nation by crossing the floor to merge his opposition party with the ruling party led by a man he had branded a military dictator.
The merger prompted accusations of betrayal and of Kim serving his own lust for power at any cost -- accusations that linger to this day.

But he neutralised the military elite within the ruling Democratic Liberal Party headed by then president Roh Tae-woo, secured the presidential nomination and swept to power in an election two years later.
Kim is now going head-on against Kim Dae-jung, leader of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, over the labour law as he did in the 1992 election.
Analysts said that by agreeing to revise the law, Kim had turned the tables and would hound the opposition for continuing a national crisis as concerns mount over the slowing economy.
On Thursday, the ruling party fired an opening salvo, calling the opposition shameless for rejecting the offer to reopen parliamentary debate over the law.

"It is really shameless behaviour...for the opposition to demand the nullification of the law, while it could not provide an alternative and has not put forward its own draft," a New Korea Party statement said.
Kim's aides argue that forced passage of the law was necessary because opposition deputies physically blocked the National Assembly speaker from opening debate on the bill several times.
Yoon Young-ho, president of Yoido Institute, a think-tank for the ruling party, said the opposition would end up on the defensive as the public wanted politicians to solve the crisis.
"The president made all the concessions. The ball is now in the opposition's court," he said.
Song Bok, social science professor at Yonsei University, said the tug-of-war for public opinion was a "lose-lose" smear campaign before the election.
"We have a self-righteous ruling camp and the opposition full of vengence," Song said. "Kim has been badly damaged by the law and now the ruling party is trying to inflict damage to the oppositon."
